title: Are Bonds Pricing In A Fed Policy Mistake?
desc:
Are Bonds Pricing In A Fed Policy Mistake?

Authored by Michael Lebowitz via RealInvestmentAdvice.com,

Imagine someone looking into their crystal ball and telling you at the beginning of October that the coming September CPI data would be higher than expected, and producer prices (PPI) would rise 1.3% for the month, well above the 0.5% forecast. On top of the bad inflation news, they also said more inflation pressure was brewing, with crude oil prices rising $10 through the first two weeks of the month. Based on that foresight, where would you guess the 10-year Treasury yield would be? To help you answer, the ten-year US Treasury yield was flirting with 5.25% on October 1. We bet most professional bond traders would have bet on 5.50% or even higher.

On October 14th, the 10-year Treasury yield surged after the CPI report, hitting 5.33% minutes after the release. A few days later, it was markedly lower at 5.03%. The 30-year yield fell by a similar amount. Bonds rallied into the teeth of the bad inflation data.

Mohamed El-Erian, ex CEO of PIMCO and renowned bond expert, asked the obvious question on X:

Why are US government bond yields falling despite hotter-than-expected CPI and PPI inflation prints?

He offered two valid rationalizations. In this article, we walk through his two AI-related explanations and add two of our own. Importantly, we emphasize one we think matters most: the bond market may be starting to price in the risk that the Fed is being pushed into a policy mistake.

Explanation One: A Flight To Quality Out Of Tech

El-Erian's first driver is a flight to quality "out of formerly high-flying tech stocks that are now coming under pressure."

  • Many semiconductor stocks have been under pressure. The SOX semiconductor index fell almost 20% between October 1 and the PPI release on the 15th.
  • The Nasdaq, with a large semiconductor weighting, fell in sympathy. Foreign markets, including the tech-heavy Korea's KOSPI and Japan's Nikkei, were also down sharply.
  • As we show below, healthcare (XLV), consumer staples (XLP) and other beaten-up value sectors have rallied since October 1, while technology (XLK) moved in the opposite direction. This rotation was primarily a flight to quality within the equity market, but El-Erian thinks it may have also sparked some bond buying.

Additionally, El-Erian notes there are "emerging pockets of credit stress in the most vulnerable segments." To his point, CoreWeave, a large data center provider, saw yields on its debt rise from 9% to 15%. Because investors are demanding such high yields for CoreWeave's debt and some of its competitors, there is a growing concern that CoreWeave might be the AI trade's canary in the coal mine.

Credit-related issues, such as those noted, often lead to a flight to quality from corporate bonds to US Treasuries.

Explanation Two: Is Tech Still A Growth Engine?

El-Erian's second driver carries broader macroeconomic implications. AI-related capital spending has been a primary engine of economic growth. If investors are less willing to fund the AI build-out, and if firms can't afford to fund it, does the economic growth outlook dim?

Saxo's Charu Chanana noted:

Investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost.

With 10-year yields above 5% and some AI-related credit spreads at junk bond levels, the cost of financing data centers has risen sharply. Less AI capex means less GDP growth, and lower expected growth argues for lower inflation, which results in lower long-term yields.

Explanation Three: Short Covering And Signs Of Significant Demand

Our first addition to El-Erian's list is short covering. The bond market entered October leaning heavily toward higher yields.

To wit, CFTC data showed asset managers added more than 100,000 contracts to their short 10-year Treasury futures exposure in the week ending September 22, one of the largest weekly additions since 2023, according to Bloomberg. Furthermore, open interest in 10-year futures rose in 13 of 14 sessions through late September, and in 5-year futures in 11 of 12 sessions. Those are consistent with new short positions being added as yields rose.

The 10- and 30-year Treasury auctions on October 7th and 8th appear to have foreshadowed the reversal. Many investors expected weak demand for the new supply of debt. They got the opposite. Per our Commentary Bond Auctions: You Never Hear About The Good Ones:

The 10-year note auction on Wednesday sold $39 billion at a 5.300% high yield. It stopped 1.7 basis points through the when-issued level, meaning it cleared much better than the market expected. Thursday's 30-year $22.5 billion bond auction was similar. The box plots below, courtesy of Exante Data, show how far outside normal both readings sit. The bid-to-cover measures the amount of dollars bid for every dollar sold. The 10-year came in at 2.77 compared to a twelve-month average of 2.51, higher than any of the last 50 auctions. The 30-year was 2.54 against a 2.40 median, at the upper edge of the last 50 auctions.

Primary dealer participation may be the most important auction statistic. The Treasury's primary dealers must bid and absorb whatever nobody else wants. When an auction has a high percentage dealer take, it means the auction struggled, and Wall Street got stuck with inventory. Dealers took a mere 2.5% of the 10-year, their lowest share on record for the tenor, and 6.8% of the 30-year. Indirect bidders, largely foreign central banks and domestic institutions, took 80.3% and 72.3%, both far above their averages.

When dealers are left buying little at Treasury auctions, as we saw, it means real money buyers are absorbing supply at these yields. While the bond market didn't rally on the strong auctions, it certainly put short sellers on notice that demand was robust at yields above 5%. The rising demand may have prompted Treasury-bond buying to cover short positions. Given how offside the market was, the buying created a circular effect, forcing more short sellers to cover.

Explanation Four: The Bond Market Smells A Policy Mistake

The bond market may be beginning to believe that this month's hot inflation data will force the Fed's hand toward more, not fewer, rate hikes, ultimately resulting in a policy error.

The yield curve's changing shape over the past two weeks supports our view. The 2yr-10yr yield curve was 57 basis points on October 7th. Following the CPI and PPI reports, it flattened to 32 basis points. That's a relatively large 25-basis-point decline in two weeks, with most of it occurring on the days of the inflation data.

When all yields decline, but long-end yields fall more than short-term yields, that is called a bull flattener. A market that expects the Fed to tighten into a weakening economy buys long bonds and flattens the curve. A market fearing runaway inflation should result in a bear steepener reaction.

The front end of the yield curve prices the odds of Fed rate hikes. The long end is pricing the consequences.

Reasons To Fret A Policy Mistake

There are a few reasons we think the bond market should worry about the Fed.

First, the recent increase in inflation is largely a supply shock. Gasoline and diesel prices are rising because of the conflict with Iran, not because consumers are overheating. The Fed can't produce oil, but it can reduce demand for everything else.

Second, the labor market is weak. September payrolls rose just 29,000 and prior months were revised down by 60,000. Furthermore, the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% and real earnings are flat to slightly negative, leaving little evidence of an inflationary wage-price spiral.

Third, consumers are being squeezed. The most recent retail sales beat estimates at 0.8%, but gasoline sales drove most of the gain. To wit, the Control Group, which the BEA uses in its GDP calculation, rose only 0.1. Essentially, higher gas prices are crowding out other spending.

Fourth, Fed policy is already restrictive by the Fed's own math. The September rate hike raised Fed Funds to 3.75% to 4.00%, above the Fed's own estimate of the longer-run neutral rate at 3.20%. The median dot plots in the latest Fed Economic Projections (SEP), along with commentary from some Fed members, suggest another rate hike or two is quite possible.

Lastly, financial conditions are tightening. The 10-year yield above 5%, 30-year mortgage rates near 7.50%, an 18-month high in the dollar, and widening credit spreads are all doing the Fed's work. Fed Funds rate hikes make financial conditions even more restrictive.

The Hawks Case

To be fair, Fed hawks have a rational case for raising rates further. The recent CPI report showed broader price increases across many goods and services, core PCE running near 3%, and, probably more importantly, inflation has been above the Fed's target for more than five years. The Fed is rightly concerned about inflation expectations becoming unanchored.

But the bond market is not voting on whether inflation is too high or what it has been. It is voting on where inflation will be and whether the Fed's inflation cure will not only heal the patient of its inflation problem but bring on recessionary side effects.

Summary

Falling bond yields amid hot inflation data are not a paradox. They reflect a flight to quality out of tech, doubts about AI as a growth engine, the unwinding of crowded short positions, and strong demand.

Most importantly, in our view, they signal concern that the Fed is responding to an energy-driven inflation shock and that inflation has been too high for too long, tightening into a slowing economy. The shape of the yield curve and the direction of long-end yields offer a good roadmap for what may happen next.

title: Clinton-Nominated Judge Says DOGE Illegally Accessed Data On Government Workers

Clinton-Nominated Judge Says DOGE Illegally Accessed Data On Government Workers

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

A federal judge ruled on Oct. 20 that a department aimed at making the government more efficient should not have been granted access to sensitive federal employee data.

Granting Department of Governmental Efficiency (DOGE) personnel access to government employee data contained in Office of Personnel Management systems violated the Privacy Act, which bars certain record disclosures and requires safeguards when disclosing other records, U.S. District Judge Denise Cote said in a 39-page ruling that granted plaintiffs final judgment.

"The defendants barely defend its legality, relying instead on what has happened since to argue that the case is moot and that prospective relief is unnecessary," wrote Cote, a judge for the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.

Department of Justice lawyers had argued in court filings that DOGE agents needed access to the records as part of an effort to modernize government systems. The government did not explain why the modernization efforts required access to the sensitive records containing personally identifiable information, according to Cote.

Lawyers had also said that the agents were granted access in case they needed the data later, but the government has never linked the access to any of the agents' duties, the ruling stated.

The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

President Donald Trump established DOGE shortly after taking office in 2025, and DOGE employees worked with various agencies to streamline operations.

Cote in June 2025 entered a preliminary injunction blocking the department from accessing federal employee records as the case proceeded, finding violations of the Privacy Act.

Professional groups, including the Association of Administrative Law Judges, brought the case and said DOGE's disclosure of employee personal data was illegal.

Twenty DOGE employees received access to Office of Personnel Management (OPM) systems from Jan. 20, 2025, to March 6, 2025, according to court documents. Some worked for OPM, but others received paychecks from other agencies.

Certain DOGE personnel had access to the systems through September 2025.

Only one of the agents remains at the office, according to the government, and he does not have access to systems containing personal employee data. DOGE itself shut down in July 2026.

The Office of Personnel Management has updated its disclosure policies, including specifying that only office employees and contractors, not detailees, can access those systems.

Cote said the updates were admirable but seemed to track with deadlines in the litigation. She also said the case was about misconduct stemming from "the failure of particular individuals," not deficient procedures.

Cote said it's unclear whether any relief is necessary at this juncture, given the developments surrounding DOGE and the office. She said she would be asking the parties to offer views on what relief, if any, is appropriate.

"In the meantime, the parties are encouraged to confer and explore whether they can reach an agreement on an appropriate resolution," she said.

Authored by Dorothy Li via The Epoch Times,

China said on Monday it would expand curbs on drone exports and restrict the sales of some heavy machinery to "sensitive countries" with which the communist regime has disputes.

Exporters will need a license to ship certain types of drones, such as those capable of traveling more than 300 km (186 miles) or flying beyond the natural line of sight, China's Ministry of Commerce said in an Oct. 19 statement, citing national security grounds. The drones' engines, operating systems, and technologies used for manufacturing will also be subjected to controls.

Other affected products include some tunnel-boring machines, walking excavators, and high-altitude concrete-spraying machines - all sophisticated machinery for building railway and road tunnels through mountains, according to a separate press release.

Decades of investment have helped China become the world's major supplier of tunnel-boring machines. Chinese media have long touted that the country makes 70 percent of such machines around the globe. Among the leading manufacturers are state-owned China Railway Engineering Equipment Group, whose website said its machines are delivered to overseas projects in 36 countries, including Italy, Australia, and Peru.

Separately, the regime's commerce ministry announced export restrictions on key components of dredgers, including heavy-duty pumps used to scoop up mud and sand from the seabed.

Overseas companies and individuals will be barred from transferring China-sourced dredger-related items to "sensitive countries and regions that have disputes with China," the ministry said.

Beijing didn't name any specific country. But some analysts, including Brookings Institution fellow Kyle Chan, said India could be a likely focus. The two neighbors have longstanding border disputes that escalated into war in the 1960s.

China has invested heavily in developing its dredger industry, with state-owned CCCC Dredging being the country's leading producer and contractor.

All three new export restrictions will be enforced beginning Nov. 18.

A ministry spokesperson said these newly added products have "clear dual-use characteristics," meaning they can be used for both military and civilian purposes. Chinese officials had already notified trading partners through export-control dialogue mechanisms ahead of the announcement, the spokesperson added.

The ministry also signaled tightened checks on dual-use products. Customs officers will detain goods and question export operators if they suspect a shipment includes controlled items. Exporters will have seven working days to respond and submit required documents such as contracts and receipts. The rules take effect immediately and also apply to cross-border e-commerce, mail, and travelers' luggage.

The expanded export controls came amid global concerns over reliance on China for raw materials and industrial products.

China restricted shipment of rare earths - a sector in which it accounts for about 70 percent of global supply - in late 2025 ahead of trade negotiations with the United States, and again earlier this year amid tensions with Japan. The sweeping restrictions have prompted the United States and other major economies to diversify the source of the supply chain critical for products ranging from smartphones and medical imaging to military equipment.

Last week, the commerce ministry unveiled sweeping export controls on dozens of technologies related to artificial intelligence as Beijing tightens controls on the strategic industry amid rivalry with the United States. Also added to the export-control list were biotechnology and technologies used to make solar equipment.

Senior U.S. and Chinese officials are set to hold a talk by November under a mechanism established at a September summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington.

They asked how the league defines "women" under Article XIII, Section 1(a) of its 2026 collective bargaining agreement. That provision states, "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA," but contains no definition of the term.

"The WNBA has just taken the first step in defining what a woman is for the sports community," Stutzman told Outkick. "By clearly labeling Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White as men, they have acknowledged that identifying as a woman does not change basic human biology."

Engelbert's letter announced no new eligibility rule, no broader policy on transgender athletes and no change to the bargaining agreement with the players' union.

"So if the league is still working through these questions, how can its commissioner be so certain about my eligibility without explaining the standards that she's applying?" he said.

In August, the league's existing "anti-hate task force," made up of team presidents and general managers, discussed transgender participation and online abuse of players. The league said at the time that it faced no immediate eligibility issues and condemned the use of the subject to demean others.

"If the task force itself has not reached a clear definition, why is the commissioner making such a definitive statement?" Freedom asked.

Asked whether Engelbert had misgendered him, Freedom said, "Yes, 100%." He added, "I just want her to respect my identity because I am telling you that I identify as a woman."

Freedom said the goal of his bid is to push the league to limit play explicitly to biological females. "This is bigger than one basketball player," he said. "Who gets to determine someone's identity? The individual, the commissioner, the medical professional, or a committee or a task force?"

title: Ken Griffin Says AI Is "Almost Certainly" A Bubble As Corporate America Opens Its Anthropic And OpenAI Bills
desc:
Ken Griffin Says AI Is "Almost Certainly" A Bubble As Corporate America Opens Its Anthropic And OpenAI Bills

The man who runs one of the world's most profitable hedge funds and America's biggest market maker has a word for the AI trade, and it starts with a "b".

Speaking at the Future of Global Markets Conference in New York on Tuesday, Citadel founder Ken Griffin told Bloomberg that investors are "almost certainly" in the midst of an artificial intelligence bubble, as many companies are still figuring out how much they will spend on the technology and what, exactly, they are getting for it.

"Corporate America has been very uneven in its ability to extract value from its AI models. I think all of Corporate America is looking at their bills from Anthropic and OpenAI and going, 'Okay, we need to think about how to make sure we're getting productivity out of this.'"

That could be a problem because as BCA Research showed this week, so far AI has not produced an economy-wide acceleration in productivity growth. In fact, adjusted for shifts in utilization rates, total factor productivity growth was zero in Q2. Said otherwise, there has been zero productivity boost from AI!

And just in case anyone thought that was a throwaway line:

"Any radical transformation of our economy is generally intertwined with a bubble. These bubbles, if we want to use that word, often coincide with these giant technological transformations."

In other words, the best-paid man in the room thinks the room is in a bubble, and he is fine saying so out loud. Which, for regular readers, will sound familiar: we have been warning since last October that the AI boom runs on debt, and lately the market has started doing the warning for us.

To be sure, nobody will care this is a bubble... until the market crashes, at which point everyone will scream how nobody warned them in advance. And just like that the new TBTF is born.

"Looking At Their Bills"

Griffin's timing was impeccable, maybe a little too impeccable. Hours earlier, the WSJ reviewed a fresh draft of Anthropic's S-1, which we broke down in "Anthropic's Updated S-1: An $80.7BN Half-Year Loss, A $750BN Compute-Tab, And A 'Catastrophic Incident' Warning." The short version: Anthropic booked $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, posted an $80.7 billion GAAP net loss (about $72 billion of which is a non-cash revaluation of financing instruments, leaving a still-hefty ~$8.7 billion underlying loss), and has signed more than $600 billion of mostly noncancelable compute contracts, with talks under way for another $150 billion. That would take the tab to as much as $750 billion.

Our reaction to the revenue headline was, well, brief:

*ANTHROPIC HAD $16.3B IN REVENUE IN FIRST HALF OF 2026: WSJ that's it?

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 20, 2026

Here is what that looks like on one chart: eventually someone has to pay for the blue bars, and Griffin just told us the customers are starting to check the invoices.

Griffin, for his part, said Anthropic's success will ultimately depend on proving to investors that its models are a must-have across every industry. That is a tall order when the price of the product keeps falling (and that ignores the fact that as "every industry" finds models are indispensably, it fires "almost every" worker currently employed, leading to a labor depression) . As we showed last week, Anthropic's token prices have tumbled to an all-time low:

Falling prices and decelerating growth are a tricky combination for a company with fixed, ten-year take-or-pay obligations. It is also why IPO investors marked the valuation down to $1.5 trillion last week after Anthropic's Q3 numbers showed the sequential growth rate hitting the brakes. Put differently, the bill keeps rising and the price per unit keeps falling, and the gap is what the IPO is supposed to fund.

From "Garbage" To "Depressed" To "Golden Era"

To be fair to Griffin, his AI views have had quite a year. Speaking in Davos in January, he called AI garbage, per Bloomberg. By May he told an audience at Stanford Business School that he was depressed by everything AI could achieve. On Tuesday he struck a sunnier tone, arguing the technology will unleash a wave of new business formation in the US:

"You're seeing the threat to white collar jobs playing out; as a business owner, you're seeing your competitive moats be filled in by bulldozers. At the same time, you're thinking that this will be a golden era for entrepreneurs."

Garbage, then depressing, then a golden era that happens to be a bubble. Three views in ten months is roughly how the market has traded AI too, so maybe he is just being consistent.

Griffin also pointed back to the days before the dot-com crash and some of the "fanciful" business models of that era:

"The companies that are on the other side of that bubble are the market leaders for decades to come. I just wish I'd kept my Amazon stock in that moment."

A fair point, with one footnote: anyone who kept their Amazon stock through that moment first had to sit through a drawdown of more than 90%. The winners on the other side of a bubble tend to get there the hard way.

Goldman: Breadth Is At Its Narrowest Since The Dot-Com Bubble

Griffin isn't the only one reaching for the 2000 analogy. Goldman's chief US equity strategist Ben Snider, in his latest US Weekly Kickstart (available to pro subs), notes that with the S&P 500 just 2% from its record high but the median S&P 500 stock 15% from its high, Goldman's preferred measure of breadth "remains near its narrowest level since the Dot-Com Bubble."

Snider also tackles the "productivity" question Griffin raised, from the earnings side. He expects S&P 500 EPS growth to slow from 29% in 2026 to 18% in 2027 (adjusting for accounting distortions), and warns that "slowing AI investment growth will be a fading tailwind." How big a tailwind? Goldman's Asia sales desk (Dani Wojdyla) puts it bluntly in this week's "Positioning Reset" note: "AI capex is currently contributing about half of S&P 500 EPS growth," an impulse Goldman expects "to diminish as capex growth slows and depreciation builds."

Translation: half of the earnings growth the market is paying for comes from companies spending money on AI, which shows up as someone else's revenue... and eventually as everyone's depreciation. The early Q3 read already shows the slope turning: 53% of S&P firms have beaten consensus EPS so far, above the 25-year average of 50% but well below the 64% rate of the past four quarters.

Last week Goldman's Tony Pasquariello argued breadth "isn't so bad"... then brought up the dot-com bubble twice, including a 2027 supply wildcard that could lift net US equity supply by the most since 2000. Anthropic's IPO, of course, is a big chunk of that wildcard.

Over at BofA, Michael Hartnett's team has done the bubble math on concentration. Peak concentration in the major bubbles of the past two centuries clustered around 40% (railroads were the outlier at 63%). The "AI Big 10" (Mag 7 plus Broadcom, AMD and Micron) recently hit 42%, above the 41% TMT peak in 2000:

Nothing says "healthy market" like a chart where the current reading sits between the Nifty Fifty and Japan in 1989.

Credit Got There First

If equity investors are only now discovering the word "bubble", the credit market has been pricing it for weeks. Per Goldman credit strategist Amanda Lynam's Global Credit Trader, "AI, Credit, and a Higher Cost of Capital" (also available to pro subs), USD HY AI-related spreads widened 25bp to 360bp over Treasuries, compared with just 2bp for non-AI issuers, with data center issuers leading the way:

Even Goldman's strategists, who just moved tactically overweight equities in their latest GOAL Kickstart, concede the point in the same note:

"Concerns on AI capex returns and funding are increasingly showing up in credit: CCC-BB spreads, hyperscaler CDS and neocloud OAS have all widened, with the latest move particularly sharp for neocloud issuers."

So Goldman is long the stocks and short the credit, while the credit is the one sending the warning. Their own Risk Appetite Indicator just "turned negative for the first time since March 2026," with all five sub-components down over the past month. Bullish, maybe... but not exactly confident.

The equity-credit gap is stark. As Goldman's basket desk showed in a chart we highlighted in "Trick Or Treat", hyperscaler equities were about 15% lower the last time hyperscaler credit spreads were this wide:

And the debt pile is only getting bigger. Goldman's credit team expects project finance plus direct hyperscaler issuance to hit $720 billion in 2027, up from $37 billion of project finance in all of 2025, with risks "firmly skewed to the upside":

The cracks are already showing where capital meets reality. Korea's Elice cratered 32% on its debut despite a retail tranche 400 times oversubscribed, and Australia's Nextdc imploded 45% and is mulling force majeure as protesters stall power to its Melbourne campus. Here is the updated casualty list:

Fink: The Bubble Can't Stop Inflating

Not everyone in the C-suite agrees with Griffin, or rather they agree, they just don't see any way out. Less than a day after the Citadel CEO's comments, BlackRock's Larry Fink took the opposite side, warning on Bloomberg TV from the Berlin Global Dialogue that the real danger is building too slowly. Per Bloomberg:

"If we don't build out these data centers, it is actually more inflationary because the cost of compute is so high right now. And the faster we can build out more data centers, the more compute we have, the faster we can bring down the cost."

Incidentally, this is precisely the point we made a month ago:

The more data centers are lit, the faster this bubble pops

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) September 25, 2026

And, just to raise the stakes, Fink added that "If we slow down the build out of this technology, I think it really does jeopardize the economy." (Deutsche Bank's Christian Sewing, for what it's worth, also played down Griffin's bubble fears on Wednesday.)

Translation: the bubble is too important to stop inflating. Coming from the head of a firm whose infrastructure arm is among the biggest data center buyers on the planet, maybe that is not a huge surprise.

Fink does have a point on the physical bottleneck, and it is one we have been hammering for months: the constraint is power, permits and angry neighbors, which is why we keep arguing that "behind the meter" generation should be mandatory for new campuses. Nextdc's Melbourne fiasco is exactly that constraint in action, and so are the billions in Nvidia chips collecting dust in Amazon warehouses because there is nowhere to plug them in.

But the rest of his argument runs into the numbers above. If compute is so scarce and expensive, it is odd that Anthropic's token prices just hit an all-time low and its revenue growth is slowing (thank Chinese open-source models, which Dario is desperate to ban at the sovereign level). More importantly, building faster means borrowing faster, and Fink himself flagged the problem in the same interview:

"We're at a time now where we're finally unlocking private capital, and so the competition for capital is as large as I've ever seen in my professional career."

He also said bond yields are "flashing," adding: "Wake up, federal government. Our deficits are starting to have real large issues." Put the two together and you get the trade-off we have been describing for months: every extra dollar of AI debt is competing with Uncle Sam's ~$2 trillion deficit for the same duration buyers, with the 10Y already above 5%. As we noted on Sept 1, AI issuance has been crowding out Treasuries. In other words, Fink's cure for compute inflation (build more, faster, with borrowed money) is a fine recipe for bond-market inflation.

Who Holds The Bag On The Other Side?

Griffin's bubble call comes with a familiar bullish escape hatch: bubbles fund revolutions, and the survivors become the Amazons of the next two decades. That is probably right about the technology. It says very little about the price anyone pays to get there, or about who ends up holding the paper when the bills come due.

Griffin says it's a bubble; Fink says stopping it would be inflationary. Both can be right, which is precisely the problem. And right now the bills are piling up on both sides. On one side, Anthropic needs public investors to backstop as much as $750 billion of compute it has already promised to pay for. On the other, its biggest customers (per Griffin) are starting to ask what they are getting for their money. Meanwhile half of S&P earnings growth depends on the capex continuing, the credit market is already charging more to fund it, and the bond market (per Fink himself) is "flashing."

So we'll side with Griffin's first word over his last one. The AI buildout will probably produce a few generational winners, but the path from here to there looks a lot more like 2000-2002 than like a "golden era", and as usual, credit is telling equities which way the bubble deflates. If the man with the best seat in the house wishes he had kept his Amazon shares, maybe the more useful lesson is that he didn't buy more of them in March 2000.

title: Bolivia's Energy Crisis Deepens As Natural Gas Reserves Run Dry
desc:
Bolivia's Energy Crisis Deepens As Natural Gas Reserves Run Dry

Authored by Felicity Bradstock via OilPrice,

  • Bolivia's dwindling natural gas reserves and declining exports have undermined its economy and intensified fuel shortages.
  • Rising global energy prices and subsidy cuts have increased living costs and fueled widespread protests.
  • A $1.9 billion IMF rescue package and energy-sector reforms aim to stabilize the economy, but long-term recovery requires diversification.

Years of underinvestment in Bolivia's gas industry have left the South American country facing a severe fuel shortage, as energy prices rise ever higher owing to the ongoing war in Iran. The energy shortages and economic crisis follow years of poor decision-making by the government.

In 2006, then-president Evo Morales took control of Bolivia's fossil fuel industry, renegotiating contracts with international oil and gas companies and benefiting from the revenue. Much of the country's newfound wealth was invested in public spending programs, expensive fuel subsidies, and the maintenance of a fixed currency exchange rate pegged to the U.S. dollar. Fossil fuel revenues contributed heavily to Bolivia's economy for several years, supporting GDP expansion and the development of social programs that helped halve poverty rates.

For many years, Bolivian's were led to believe that they had more extensive gas supplies than they actually did. However, in recent years, Bolivia's fossil fuel sector has suffered as reserves have dwindled and no successful gas discoveries have occurred. As of April, Bolivia has an estimated 3.7 trillion cubic feet of proven reserves. The fall in gas production led exports to fall by almost 60 percent over the last decade. Bolivia continues to rely heavily on natural gas, which accounts for around 70 percent of its electricity mix.

Meanwhile, little progress has been made in developing the country's green energy sector, leaving it facing severe energy shortages. The fall in gas revenues has left the economy suffering terribly, as inflation soars and the price of imported goods becomes ever more unaffordable. Luis Fernando Romero, the former head of an association of economists in southern Bolivia, stated, "We failed to take advantage of a historic opportunity that brought in immense revenue."

This situation is not uncommon, with many other oil-rich states having had similar experiences. Several Middle Eastern states have long depended on oil and gas revenues for economic growth, and most have only recently announced plans to diversify their economies to reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Several countries across the MENA region announced new economic strategies following greater talk of a global green transition, which could leave them missing out on vital oil revenues if they don't take moves to diversify and invest in value-added sectors.

The lack of investment in Bolivia's other domestic sectors has left it struggling to stay afloat as it runs out of fuel and is forced to pay high fuel import costs. President Rodrigo Paz warned that "International prices are forcing us to make complex choices."

In September, Bolivia's Congress approved a $1.9 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), even though the terms of the deal require the government to impose strict austerity measures that could fuel social unrest. The loan received approval from the IMF's Executive Board on October 2, and the government will now be required to cut its fuel subsidies and significantly reduce public spending. It has already increased fuel prices and is expected to scrap further gasoline subsidies from the beginning of next year. The loan is expected to unlock up to $4 billion more in financing from the World Bank and other lenders.

However, there are major concerns that the new financial plan will significantly increase the cost of living for households already struggling. Last December, the government reduced fuel subsidies, leaving little support for the most vulnerable Bolivians. This led to widespread protests as people called for President Paz's resignation. In February, there was further social unrest after the distribution of poor-quality gasoline ruined thousands of vehicles. Then, in June and July, several weeks of road blockades by protesters occurred.

Meanwhile, to tackle the ongoing fuel shortages, Bolivia's government announced plans in September to triple the fund financing refined fuel purchases, following similar announcements by Peru and Ecuador. This is expected to help mitigate diesel shortages and rising prices. Both Peru and Ecuador have increased fuel subsidies in recent months and are focusing on increasing production at state oil refineries to alleviate the price pressure of expensive fuel imports.

In July, Bolivia's Energy Minister Marcelo Blanco announced that the government had authorized the private sector to import and sell refined fuels to mitigate severe shortages. Then, in September, the government said that the state hydrocarbons firm plans to focus on exploration, extraction, and refining to continue developing Bolivia's gas resources. However, experts warn that Bolivia could become a net fossil gas importer by around 2030.

As Bolivia continues to battle fuel shortages and seeks to support economic recovery by borrowing from international organizations, the government must focus on diversifying the economy by developing other value-added sectors to sustain long-term growth. In addition, the government must also develop Bolivia's renewable energy sources to reduce dependence on expensive fuel imports and ensure the country's energy security.

title: Japan's Electricity Prices Surge 25% As LNG And Coal Costs Soar
desc:
Japan's Electricity Prices Surge 25% As LNG And Coal Costs Soar

Authored by Tsvetana Paraskova via OilPrice,

Japan's average power prices jumped by over 25% at the start of this week from the previous week amid soaring LNG and higher coal prices.

The nationwide power price rose by over 25% week-to-week to $0.19 (31.15 Japanese yen) per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Monday, Bloomberg reported, citing data from Japan Electric Power Exchange.

Japan, one of the world's biggest LNG importers, this summer reduced gas-fired generation in favor of coal as the price of liquefied natural gas remained elevated.

Japan has been burning more coal and less gas for power generation since the war in the Middle East started, and it is not the only one. All Asian countries have made the switch from gas to coal on affordability and availability grounds.

Moreover, surging oil prices have led to a significant increase in Japan's import bill for oil and LNG.

LNG prices surged in Asia to a four-year high as very few cargoes manage to exit the Strait of Hormuz while competition with Europe for winter supply is intensifying.

The average spot LNG price for delivery into north-east Asia in December was assessed at $29.30 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) at the end of last week. This was the highest spot LNG price for Asia since December 2022, and sharply higher compared to $26.50 per MMBtu assessed in the previous week.

As a result, Japan's gas-fueled power generation is the most expensive in years.

The switch to coal, for its part, has also had its cost challenges this year. Increased demand in Asia amid reduced supply from the top thermal coal exporter, Indonesia, is driving up coal prices, too. The global benchmark for coal prices, the Newcastle futures, have jumped by 30% compared to pre-war levels.

Power prices in Japan have also jumped this month due to scheduled maintenance at some power-generating facilities ahead of winter.

Federal prosecutors plan to use DNA evidence in their criminal investigation of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), people familiar with the probe told the New York Post on Monday. One source said the DNA is critical to proving the long-running allegation that Omar's 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi was a marriage to her brother, made so he could get a green card he never received. Omar has denied the claim since 2016, no charges have been filed, and the Justice Department has not confirmed any DNA evidence.

The DNA report is the latest turn in a probe that went public a week ago, when Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Omar's Washington home on Oct. 12. Agents also seized Omar's phone, and more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas have gone out, some to her relatives, a source told the Associated Press. The grand jury is collecting evidence in Minnesota, where the U.S. Attorney's Office opened the case. Omar called the search an "attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement" and said, "I will not be silenced."

The Post's sources did not say whether the DNA was collected before or after the search. One of them pushed back on earlier reports that investigators went "dumpster diving" for swabs of Omar, Elmi or family members. Reporter Leland Vittert had said on Saturday that agents had done just that, before the raid:

Multiple sources have confirmed to me that federal agents went dumpster diving to get DNA from Minnesota Congresswoman @IlhanMN and her family before the raid on her D.C. home earlier this week. Our reporting suggests investigations go far beyond simple immigration fraud. NewsNation sources say the likely coming indictments will be stunning in nature and far beyond anything the public has understood the case to be about.

— Leland Vittert (@LelandVittert) October 17, 2026

Two other sources told the Post that the search, the DNA and other evidence give prosecutors a solid basis to bring a charge of conspiracy to commit immigration fraud before a grand jury. A conspiracy charge would let prosecutors allege overt acts that fall outside the statute of limitations, former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani told the Post. He said prosecutors could pursue a conspiracy case that would likely fall within a 10-year limit, or a civil case, which has none, and that the warrant would not have been executed unless it had "come from the highest levels of the DOJ."

That fits the warrant. A person familiar with the document told The Washington Post that it lists potential charges of conspiracy, immigration fraud and false statements. Investigators are also looking at whether Omar or her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, misstated her birth date on immigration paperwork so she could derive citizenship through him when he naturalized in 2000. Rahmani called her late father "an unindicted co-conspirator." The Justice Department has not released the affidavit.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose department's agents carried out the search, said on Oct. 16 that "multiple other warrants" were served the same day. "We had a judge sign it, and we expect to be able to take the case to a grand jury," he told the Charlie Kirk Show, according to CBS News.

The marriage and the birth-date theory lead to different places. A marriage-fraud conviction would not threaten Omar's own citizenship the way a false-statements case would, the New York Post noted, and stripping the citizenship of a sitting member of Congress would be unprecedented. Border czar Tom Homan said over the weekend that the government has built "a strong case" that could lead the administration to seek denaturalization. As we reported, the Wall Street Journal had already said officials wanted to revoke her citizenship and deport her, and agents reportedly secured her passport in the search.

D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, whose office is separately examining Omar's House financial disclosures, told Fox News that "that judge would not have signed that warrant unless there was probable cause." Those disclosures cut Omar's reported net worth by tens of millions of dollars in a year, which the Post attributed to an unexplained accounting "discrepancy."

Omar's lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, answered last week with a letter to the Justice Department demanding the "immediate return" of everything seized. They wrote that agents ignored a magistrate judge's "special requests" for carrying out the search and broke longstanding DOJ policy by acting so close to an election, and that President Trump has "made no secret" of wanting to target her. A DOJ spokesperson called the letter "riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies" and said leaking it was "a publicity play." Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on House Judiciary, had already called the search "blatant political intimidation," coming 22 days before the Nov. 3 election. Former federal prosecutor Jim Trusty told Fox News the warrant shows "at least probable cause," but that it is "a long way off from proving a case at trial."

The marriage record at the heart of the DNA claim is tangled. Omar and Elmi divorced in 2017, and she gave birth to her third child while legally married to him. Her marriage to Ahmed Hirsi was not legally entered into until after her divorce from Elmi was finalized, the Post reported, although the two had a Muslim ceremony in 2002. She filed joint taxes with Hirsi in 2014 and 2015 while still legally married to Elmi, from whom she had separated in 2011. Elmi, who lives in the UK, applied for a marriage-based green card and withdrew it in 2019 when immigration officials asked for more evidence, according to The Washington Post, which also quoted a former immigration official saying the brother claim was investigated during Trump's first term without enough evidence to go forward. Omar divorced Hirsi in 2019 and married political consultant Tim Mynett.

We reported last week that her staff asked Minnesota's legislative library in 2019 to change her birth year, and that Mynett snapped at a reporter over rumors she had fled the country. Mynett has said only that his wife "came here when she was 12 years old as a child war refugee." Her lawyers say there is "no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status."

"Federal student aid is intended to expand educational opportunities, not line the pockets of fraudsters who steal from students pursuing their education and hardworking taxpayers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the statement.

"Treasury is working with financial institutions and law enforcement to identify these fraud schemes, recover stolen funds, and hold those responsible accountable."

The department said it was working with the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, headed by Vice President JD Vance, and encouraging whistleblowers to report fraud-related information.

In an example of educational fraud, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced last month that a Detroit man was sentenced to 92 months in federal prison for fraud schemes, including one that targeted federal student aid programs.

The man and others submitted fraudulent student aid claims for more than 1,200 individuals, collecting more than $10 million before being caught, the DOJ said. The fraud spanned 100 schools across more than 20 states.

In March, the DOJ said a former professor admitted to stealing government funds through a scam involving fraudulent student financial aid applications. More than 100 such false applications were filed across several universities and colleges in Texas.

Education Aid Schemes

The Treasury detailed some of the federal student aid fraud schemes in its statement. For instance, "ghost student" schemes involve criminals stealing an individual's personal information and using it to enroll as a student in classes. The victim often never realizes that a third party is collecting student aid in their name.

In "straw student" schemes, fraudsters pay real people to enroll in classes and collect financial aid in their names. In some cases, corrupt school employees may be part of these schemes.

"Student aid fraud has real consequences for students and American taxpayers. It drains finite grant resources from deserving students, potentially prevents legitimate students from enrolling in classes occupied by fraudulent enrollees, and can leave identity theft victims responsible for debts they never incurred," the Treasury said.

In July, the Department of Education held a first-of-its-kind Higher Education Fraud Summit, with participants discussing ways to tackle fraud in the sector.

"We have already prevented nearly $2 billion in attempted federal student aid fraud from going to bad actors. Every dollar lost to fraud is a dollar taken away from a student trying to build a better future," Underssecretary of Education Nicholas Kent said in a statement.

In an October 2025 update, the University of Alaska warned students to protect themselves from student aid fraud. Specifically, the university said that students should share their personal information only with trusted, secure websites.

The university recommended that students regularly monitor their credit for any unusual or new activity and report any identity theft or other suspicious activity.

"Treat digital content, like emails, texts, voicemails, and website content, with increased scrutiny, especially if the materials or resources they provide or advertise seem too good to be true or appear designed to create a sense of urgency," the university said.

title: The Great Rare Earth Disconnect: Prices Up 23%, Miners Down 28%
desc:
The Great Rare Earth Disconnect: Prices Up 23%, Miners Down 28%

Here is a question that should be harder to answer than it is: China still controls the rare earth spigot, the latest Trump-Xi summit did nothing to loosen its grip, Japan is about to run out of yttrium, Washington has put a $110/kg floor under NdPr, and Western buyers are paying anywhere from 5x to 346x the Chinese price for heavy rare earths.

So why are rare earth stocks down on the year?

That is the question Canaccord's critical minerals team led by Reg Spencer asks in an overnight note titled "Rare Earths: Equity disconnect from strong market fundamentals", and the answer is blunt:

Given our favourable SxD outlook, floor pricing, recent pricing stability (NdPr), and Western pricing premiums (particularly for heavies), we think recent equity performance has been driven more so by global macro factors and highlights a disconnection from rare earth market fundamentals.

In other words, the commodity is acting like a strategic asset and the stocks are trading like a risk-off casualty. The numbers are stark: year to date, the ex-China NdPr price is up 23%, while Canaccord's rare earth developers are down 17% on average and its producers are down 28%.

We have been tracking the rare earth theme since long before China started rationing exports to the West in late 2024, and back in July 2025 we laid out "The Coming Rare Earth Revolution And How To Profit", flagging MP Materials as the stock best positioned to benefit. A few hours later the Pentagon announced its MP deal, and well we allowed ourselves a modest victory lap:

Last night we said MP is the stock best positioned to capitalize on the rare earth revolution. Up 43% this morning

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) July 10, 2025

Fifteen months later, MP trades at $40.17, about half of Canaccord's $82 target. So what happened?

The Chart That Says It All

Canaccord's chart below shows the problem in one picture. Chinese NdPr (black) and Rotterdam NdPr (dark blue) have converged and climbed steadily all year, with the Western price now above $110/kg. Meanwhile the REMX ETF (light blue) peaked in May and has since slid from above $100 to the high-$50s.

The carnage is broad. On the producer side, Lynas, MP, USA Rare Earth and Iluka are all deep in the red, and even China Northern Rare Earth and Shenghe are lower on the year. Diversification at its finest.

Developers did a bit better on average, mostly thanks to Viridis (VMM), which is still up well over 50% on the year. Strip that out and the picture is grim: Hastings is down roughly two-thirds, St George about half, and Arafura and Brazilian Rare Earths 35-50%.

Canaccord's verdict: "We question how equities have performed so poorly YTD despite strong underlying market fundamentals." Those fundamentals include recent sector M&A, direct government support, a scarcity of Western supply and "ex-China NdPr pricing up 23% YTD."

The Floor Works... Just Ask China

Start with the most important structural change of the past year. As we reported when the Department of Defense set a price floor last August, Washington has moved from financing Western supply to underwriting its economics. Canaccord tallies the floors: US$110/kg NdPr for MP (DoD), Lynas (Japan, US, plus upside sharing) and USA Rare Earth, which also gets US$575/kg for dysprosium and US$2,050/kg for terbium.

And the floor has done something nobody expected: it has tamed the Chinese price too. For years Beijing used export quotas, policy changes and, more recently, export controls to whipsaw NdPr from about $175/kg down to around $50 and back again. Over the past 10 months, Canaccord notes, Chinese pricing has "begun to normalise around the US$110/kg floor price level."

Put differently, the volatility that made rare earth projects unbankable has largely vanished, and yet investors are paying less for those projects than they did in January.

Two Markets, Two Prices

NdPr is now a one-price market, more or less. Everything heavier is a different story. Since Beijing started rationing heavies, the West has developed its own (thin, opaque) price for anything China won't ship, and the gaps are absurd. Rotterdam dysprosium sits around $1,074/kg vs $227 in China, and terbium at $4,594 vs $983.

But Dy and Tb are the tame ones. Canaccord now forecasts yttrium, gadolinium and samarium for the first time, and the Western premiums there are almost comical. Chinese yttrium oxide has averaged about $8/kg over the past five years, while European spot is "~US$740/kg", a premium of 85x, and "some price reporting agencies have quoted US prices of up to US$1,750/kg." Gadolinium trades about 10x China in Baltimore, with US CIF quotes as high as $3,100/kg.

We ran Canaccord's own spot price table through the calculator, and here is what the "dual market" looks like element by element. CIF North America samarium, used in the SmCo magnets that go into missiles, fighter jets and radar, trades at 346 TIMES THE CHINESE PRICE!

And the squeeze is very real. Just this morning the FT reported that Japan has made an urgent request to Washington and global companies to help resolve its yttrium crisis, warning of a severe shortage by year-end. "Inventories are plummeting," one official said. Per Argus, yttrium oxide costs about $9/kg in China and roughly $1,150/kg outside it, a 179-fold jump in two years. A senior US official added that China is shipping the US just two-thirds of the rare earths it promised under last October's truce, and Japan "only the bare minimum." That followed last month's Trump-Xi summit, where China pledged to buy US coal but fell short on rare earths, and the two sides settled for a two-month truce that markets promptly faded.

To be fair, Canaccord is careful here. It notes the ex-China DyTb market was just 151 tonnes in 2025, and China's was 22x larger. It warns that Western premiums "should be viewed cautiously" and that "we question whether pricing is sustainable at these levels," with some magnet makers already pivoting to lower-cost ferrite magnets. Its own price deck has ex-China yttrium falling from $740/kg this year to $100 by 2030. Still, even the bank's haircut numbers leave Western producers with integrated separation (it names Lynas and MP) earning premiums nobody would have modeled two years ago.

Demand Goes Up, Again

Meanwhile the demand side keeps getting revised higher. Canaccord now sees NdFeB magnet demand growing at a 7.3% CAGR to ~365,000 tonnes by 2035, 15% above its prior update. EVs remain the anchor (52 million units by 2035 vs 23.5 million in 2026), but the bank has added data centers (motors for cooling), e-bikes and scooters, and drones. Drones are only ~1% of forecast demand, but the bank notes that Ukrainian and Russian military drone production alone was estimated at ~9 million units, so "our model forecasts may prove conservative."

Then there are the robots. Canaccord models humanoid deliveries growing at a 45% CAGR to 2.5 million units by 2035, and points out that Tesla is reportedly preparing an Optimus line designed for 1 million robots a year. For comparison, global EV sales rose more than 4,600% from 2014 to 2024. Maybe the robot curve won't look like that... but if it does, the magnet math gets very ugly very quickly.

Netting it all out, Canaccord sees the global NdPr market in deficit through 2028 (about 7% short this year), roughly balanced in 2029-31 as Eneabba, Kangankunde, Caldeira, White Mesa and the Lynas expansions come online, and then sliding back into a deeper deficit: -10% by 2035. Dy+Tb follows the same shape, ending at a 12% deficit.

The West's Blind Spot

The bulls' case gets even stronger once you look past the mines. Canaccord forecasts ex-China NdFeB magnet capacity rising more than 300% by 2030 to about 70,000 tonnes, which sounds impressive until you realize it would still be only 23% of global capacity, with China at ~77%.

And the West may not even get there, because it is missing a step. Global NdFeB metallisation and alloying capacity is about 210,000 tonnes in 2026, and more than 90% of it is Chinese controlled. Ex-China capacity is set to roughly double to 38,000 tonnes by 2030, which falls well short of planned Western magnet capacity. Canaccord calls metallisation "a major blind spot in western supply chain development", and its channel checks found lead times of up to two years for strip casters, "with sourcing from China impossible under current export controls."

This echoes ING's warning, which we covered two weeks ago, that China's rare earth chokehold may outlast this decade because the bottleneck is "industrial rather than geological." Canaccord's conclusion is just as stark: "our research points to China maintaining market dominance, with shortfalls in Western supply (and likelihood of ongoing Chinese export controls) supporting bifurcated markets and pricing premiums."

Translation: the scarcity premium for anything mined, separated or metallised outside China is a structural feature that will be around for years, and the companies capturing it are trading as if it will be gone by next quarter.

Wall Street Is Paying 50 Cents On The Dollar

Which brings us to valuation. Canaccord's producer coverage trades at an average 0.57x P/NAV and its developers at 0.47x. On the bank's targets, MP has 104% upside, Lynas 108% (target raised to A$23), USA Rare Earth 204% and Energy Fuels 150%, even after Canaccord cut its EFR target to C$30 on project delays.

The rating changes: Meteoric (MEI) goes to Hold from Spec Buy, since its value is now tied to Lynas' all-scrip takeover at 0.0207 LYC shares per MEI share. (Lynas shares fell almost 8% the day that deal was announced, another reminder that this market keeps punishing consolidation.) Hastings (HAS) goes to Spec Buy from Hold "on valuation", even though its target was cut to A$0.30 from A$0.55, which tells you just how far the stock has fallen.

Of course, price targets have a habit of following prices rather than leading them, and at least some of the selloff has a perfectly sensible explanation: these are long-duration, capex-heavy projects at a time when the 10Y is above 5%, tech is wobbling and the bid for anything speculative has evaporated. Canaccord concedes as much, blaming "global macroeconomic pressures."

Same Disconnect, Different Metal

Tungsten isn't a rare earth, but it is a critical material with the same chokepoint (China controls roughly 80% of supply, per Jefferies), and it shows the exact same disconnect, only worse. Take Almonty Industries (ALM), the most prominent Western tungsten miner and a name we have covered extensively in recent weeks.

When Goldman's Nick Cash initiated coverage last month, he put Almonty "at the center of the Western tungsten investment narrative," with tungsten prices up 8x since the start of 2025. He was also the Street's skeptic, expecting prices to normalize and Sangdong's ramp to run slower than the market hoped, with a $13 target vs a $24.73 consensus. The stock was $12.74 that morning. Today it is below $9, down 62% from its April peak and back where it started the year, after dropping another 10% on the day of yesterday's Investor Day. So even Goldman's cautious target now implies about 45% upside.

Meanwhile the operations are going the right way. Sangdong in South Korea started production in September and is moving toward 24/7 operations, with its first concentrate shipment due later this month, and Cantor's Matthew O'Keefe models output jumping from 126,287 MTU this year to 444,400 MTU in 2027, with all-in sustaining costs falling from $905 to $319 per MTU. Oppenheimer's Ian Zaffino puts the shares at just 5.7x/4.2x FY27/FY28 EBITDA, with roughly $290 million in net cash.

So what spooked the market? Spot prices. Western APT has slipped from $3,140 to about $2,700/MTU, and Chinese prices have retreated even more sharply. But Zaffino explains why that is a misleading signal: Western APT and oxide plants are running at capacity under long-term contracts and can't absorb more concentrate, so "concentrate prices have softened, even as availability of finished APT/oxide in the West remains constrained." And the demand wave hasn't even started. On January 1, 2027, US defense procurement rules extend to tungsten mining, refining and separation, so Chinese or Russian ore processed in a third country no longer qualifies. Stifel says the US strategic tungsten stockpile is nearly depleted, and Bernstein sees the Western rearmament order boom running from 2027 through 2030. The cherry on top: on Monday, CME announced plans to launch tungsten futures by early Q1 2027 at the latest (subject to regulatory review), which tells you how seriously the market's plumbing is taking a metal that equity investors are currently dumping.

In other words, spot is pricing today's bottleneck in Western processing, and the stock is pricing spot, while the 2027 demand cliff is priced almost nowhere. Sound familiar?

Supply Security Gets The Stage In London

Goldman, for its part, thinks the debate has already shifted. Its third Global Metals & Mining Conference kicks off in London today during LME Week, bringing together the world's largest "diversified, copper, aluminium, rare earth and lithium producers." In their conference preview, Goldman's Matt Greene and the bank's mining team write that "the conversation has increasingly shifted to supply," with governments "becoming more active participants in the mining sector through faster permitting, shared infrastructure, strategic funding, price floors and direct offtake agreements, reflecting the growing importance of resource security." The question the bank poses is the right one: "whether the industry can deliver the supply that markets are increasingly pricing in."

For rare earths, the honest answer seems to be: not anytime soon, and not without China. Which is exactly why the sector's stocks probably shouldn't be trading at half of NAV.

When Macro Lets Go

We have seen this movie before. Back in March we reported that the US reportedly had just two months of rare earths left, and in July that China's "killer chokepoint" was reshaping the global economy. Each time the physical market tightened, and when Washington finally stepped in (see last July's MP deal), the equities caught up violently.

Today we have a two-month trade truce that expires January 10, a Japanese government begging for yttrium, the West's flagship tungsten miner trading below even Goldman's skeptical target ten weeks before the Pentagon's sourcing rules kick in,a floor price that has turned NdPr into a one-way bet with a safety net, and an equity market that is valuing the West's only scalable non-Chinese suppliers at roughly half of what they're worth on conservative assumptions.

Canaccord's closing line sums it up: "We expect demand to remain strong, as the West looks to secure ex-China supply and build its independence within the global magnet supply chain."

Our take: the disconnect will probably close the same way it did last summer, with a headline out of Beijing or the Pentagon, and the investors waiting for macro to give them the all-clear will be buying it 50% higher. After all, nothing cures a 0.5x P/NAV like a 346x price premium.

title: "A Good Idea": SpaceX Jumps On Blowout Quarter, Musk Confirms Committees Discussing Tesla Merger
desc:
"A Good Idea": SpaceX Jumps On Blowout Quarter, Musk Confirms Committees Discussing Tesla Merger

Update (1730ET): The earnings call has seen SPCX shares extend their after-hours gains amid a tsunami of attention-grabbing comments from Elon Musk and CFO Bret Johnsen.

Perhaps the most shocking was Musk saying that he sees between $500 billion and $1 trillion of annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027.

Then he stepped it up further:

Musk says there’s a small opportunity for SpaceX to have 20 gigawatts of AI compute online next year.

Musk says he’s been spending a lot of his time in Memphis, "often four days a week," trying to get more data center compute developed.

He’s aiming to bring in 13 gigawatts of compute by the end of next year.

And this year, he expects between 2.5 GW and 3 GW to come online.

As a reminder, (based on this quarter’s numbers) they have 1.7 GW of nameplate compute.

“We are, frankly, hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler,” Musk says, referring to demand for SpaceX data centers.

“I don’t think we’re going to have a demand issue here.”

And finally, the topic of merging Tesla and SpaceX was brought up:

"I'm tap dancing through a minefield," says Musk on the question of a merger, adding that both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea.

Musk also downplayed the move somewhat:

"“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it."

But then he adds:

"I do think there’s a lot of merit for combining the companies," Musk says, concluding that "I think it will be a good idea".

The market is pricing a 66% chance of the merger being completed by the end of next year...

All of that combined, has pushed SPCX up around 5%...

* * *

As we wrote in our preview, hopes are high for what SpaceX will report today. The company is expected to report solid revenue growth, however more than offset by far more solid capex growth which will result in SpaceX burning almost a quarter trillion over the next 3 years as it builds out its data center capacity. Notably, SpaceX could post its first quarterly profit today - though this is only its second earnings report as a public company. Wall Street expects earnings of 15 cents a share, or about $1.9 billion in net income, compared with a $541 million loss last quarter.

Besides the top and FCF lines, Deutsche's list of "other areas of focus" is a good checklist of what else to look for:

  • AI: neocloud pricing and new contracts, the Cursor contribution, Grok Bot adoption, and the data center capex outlook (read: any hint that 2027 capex starts with a "2").
  • Launch: timing of the next few launches after Flight 14; Flight 15 looks set for mid-/late November, though DB doesn't expect a second-stage catch.
  • Connectivity: after the $8 billion Grain spectrum deal, "additional color on management's next move(s) in the US (build vs. buy)," which is something the wireless carriers will be listening to closely.

Additionally, investors are seeking additional hints about a potential Tesla and SpaceX merger. Today’s earnings are happening just a few days after Tesla unveiled its new Roadster, which incorporated SpaceX gas thrusters that allowed the vehicle to hover and do barrel rolls in the air. Following the event, a bunch of Tesla and SpaceX executives and employees started following each other on X, according to an account that monitors tech executives. DB said that the timing as "mainly a function of valuation differentials and politics (may want to avoid a potential Democrat-led administration taking over post Trump)."

Elon Musk has talked a lot about the “convergence” of his businesses over the last year. Meanwhile SpaceX and Tesla are already collaborating on one of Musk’s most ambitious projects: the Terafab, which aims to mass produce semiconductor chips in the US to be used in his companies’ various products.

Don't expect to see much, if any profit: Starlink satellite-internet service is SpaceX’s only profitable business. The militarized version of Starlink, called Starshield, came under increased scrutiny last week after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the White House and Musk of placing restrictions on the technology in Ukraine, disrupting military operations. Both Musk and Trump have denied involvement, igniting a firestorm over who controls the technology that has become indispensable to Ukraine’s war against Russia.

As for the market's reaction, recall that SPCX shares slumped 14% the day after its first earnings release in August, in part over fears that insiders would sell shares after the earliest of many lockup expirations. Those fears were quickly calmed when the shares rebounded, but the setup heading into this quarter’s results is similar to last time. On Wednesday, an additional 1.3 billion shares, representing 28% of those subject to the 180-day lock-up period, will become available to trade.

So with all that in mind, here is what SpaceX just reported for Q3, its second quarter as a public company. For the most part a solid beat across the board, blowing past Wall Street expectations, and posting its first quarterly profit, $4.4 billion, or 35 cents a share, more than double estimates, while spending a massive $20 billion on capex

  • Revenue $14.58 billion, beating estimates of $12.87 billion
    • Space revenue $1.77 billion, beating estimates of $1.43 billion
    • Connectivity revenue $5.25 billion, beating estimates of $4.86 billion

Here is the revenue by segment: it shows that SpaceX is no longer a Rocket Company but is now mostly a neocloud, pardon, Hyperscaler.

  • Capital expenditure $19.59 billion, beating estimates of $19.6 billion
    • Space capital expenditure $1.61 billion, higher than estimates of $1.52 billion
    • Connectivity capital expenditure $1.54 billion, below estimates of $1.6 billion

Here is the capex by segment:

Turning to expenses...

  • Total Costs & Expenses $11.78 billion, beating estimates of $11.23 billion
  • R&D expenses $4.60 billion, missing estimates of $5.06 billion

... and operating income:

  • Operating income $2.79 billion, beating estimates of $2.24 billion
  • Connectivity operating income $2.37 billion, beating estimates of $1.86 billion
  • Adjusted Ebitda $8.81 billion, smashing estimates of $6.59 billion
    • Space adjusted Ebitda $357 million, estimate $123.1 million
    • Connectivity adjusted Ebitda $3.50 billion, estimate $2.94 billion

Here is the adjusted EBITDA by segment:

  • Number of rocket launches 35, missing estimates of 41
  • Mass to Orbit 476 mt, missing estimates of 559
  • Cash and cash equivalents $51.29 billion, estimate$91.2 billion

While much will be said about the company's profitability, note that the $4.4 billion of net income got a boost from $1 billion of “other income” and a $390 million tax benefit. That said, the underlying business still beat expectations: operating income was $2.8 billion versus $2.2 billion expected.

A visual way of representing what happened in Q3:

Looking at the key components, EBITDA and CapEx, we find that both revenue and EBITDA smashed estimates, while CapEx was largely unchanged from last quarter.

As we noted in our preview the big question would be the delta between EBITDA and CapEx growth, and as shown in the chart below, while EBITDA was a record $8.8BN, it is still nowhere near enough to catch up to the whopping $19.6BN in capex.

Another very important number: amount of installed compute rose to 1.7GW, just shy of estimates of 1.74GW.

Summarizing the fine print: SpaceX reported blowout revenues and EBITDA, driven by stronger ARPU, even as ending compute, consumer broadband subs and external launches all came below expectations.

Commenting on the quarter, the SpaceX CFO said that the company "delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business. The combination of our launch leadership, recurring Starlink revenue, and the significant expansion of our SI infrastructure continues to drive meaningful operating leverage... We are building the infrastructure of the future with discipline — focused on capital efficiency, strong returns on invested capital, and maintaining a robust, investment-grade balance sheet — while moving with the velocity to capture the opportunity in front of us."

In its wrap, Bloomberg writes that SpaceX of this quarter is not the same as the SpaceX of last quarter. AI - now officially called Super Intelligence - has overtaken Starlink to become the company’s biggest business by revenue. Just last quarter, Starlink was comfortably ahead. The speed of that shift shows just how quickly SpaceX’s AI infrastructure business is scaling.

The SpaceX story used to be rockets funding satellites. Increasingly, it’s rockets, satellites and a giant balance sheet funding an AI company. In other words, a hyperscaler.

The results were solid, and the stock liked them - at least until the call - with SPCX stock higher about 3%, fading a bit of its after hours jump.

There are two ways of looking at the midterms, now less than three weeks away.

In 1934, FDR was still riding the wave of his New Deal promises to end the Depression.

In 1998, Bill Clinton enjoyed backlash support after the Republicans’ unpopular impeachment inquiry, at a time when the economy was robust, and the budget was finally being balanced.

In 2002, George W. Bush had united the nation after 9/11 and had not yet begun what proved to be an unpopular Iraq War.

title: US Nears Russia Deal To Free Detained Americans, Witkoff En Route To Moscow
desc:
US Nears Russia Deal To Free Detained Americans, Witkoff En Route To Moscow

ABC and The New York Times are reporting that multiple Americans detained in Russia could soon be free as part of a major Trump deal with Moscow.

Negotiations are said to be in the final stages, with Special Envoy Steve Witkoff set to be in Moscow on Wednesday. And so a major announcement and release could happen by the time he leaves the Russian capital later the same day.

Stephen Hubbard, an American who is accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine forces when he was captured in 2022, is expected to be among the released prisoners.

Citing unnamed officials, ABC writes, "They add that the talks have centered on freeing Stephen Hubbard, a 72-year-old retired teacher who is the only American held in Russia officially designated as wrongfully detained by the State Department, as well as several other U.S. citizens held by Moscow on what the administration said it believes are dubious charges."

President Trump acknowledged Monday that he was "trying to get a hostage that the country has been after for a long time" - which appeared to refer to Hubbard. "Let's see what happens," Trump said. "That'll be soon."

On Tuesday, Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met in Oslo as part of efforts to find an end to the Ukraine war. In a closing presser for the talks, Zelensky said the latest working proposal features security guarantees for Ukraine modelled on NATO's Article 5, which is the collective defense clause.

"We have discussed security guarantees, and I’m grateful to the American side for emphasizing once again that they will be strong," Zelensky said following talks in Oslo.

"We discussed NATO, Article 5 and Article 5-like guarantees. Different types of security guarantees are included in the document, which Steve will share with the Russians, and we will hear their feedback."

However, the Kremlin is unlikely to go for NATO Article 5-style protections, given a key rationale for the 'special military operation' in the first place was NATO expansion up to Russia's doorstep.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has meanwhile said, "We hope that a meeting can be arranged in the very near future, and that the American negotiators, Mr. Witkoff, will be able to brief President Putin on their contacts with both the Ukrainians and the Europeans."

Norwegian PM Jonas Gahr Store says US envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to St Petersburg tomorrow for talks with the Russian leadership, following today’s discussions in Oslo with Zelensky and EU representative Alexander Stubb. “He will... exchange ideas from this meeting and proposals developed by European and American colleagues, and possibly pave the way for a meeting at the leaders’ level.”

Witkoff is due in Moscow Wednesday, where he is indeed expected to present the results of the Oslo talks to Putin and his team.

Peskov said further: "We consider such meetings to be of great importance on every occasion. They are always timely and very substantive, and we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators."
