title: Wall Street Set For Largest Bonuses In Industry History This Year
desc:
Wall Street Set For Largest Bonuses In Industry History This Year

New York's financial industry is enjoying an extraordinary earnings boom, with profits potentially topping $90 billion this year and setting the stage for the biggest round of Wall Street bonuses on record, according to Bloomberg.

According to a new analysis from State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli, securities firms generated more money during the opening six months of 2026 than in any comparable period previously recorded. If that performance continues, the industry could blow past its $65.1 billion earnings record from 2025.

Much of the surge has come from a revival in investment banking and exceptionally lucrative trading conditions. Revenue associated with underwriting jumped 68% in the first half, while advisory and account-management businesses posted a 16.4% increase. Goldman Sachs has been among the major beneficiaries, recently reporting $7.42 billion in quarterly stock-trading revenue, its third straight quarterly record in that business.

Bloomberg writes that the financial sector's success is providing a substantial boost to New York's employment figures and government finances. After reaching 207,400 workers last year, the industry is projected to expand its workforce by approximately 5,300 employees in 2026.

The state's dependence on Wall Street has also become increasingly pronounced. Securities-related business and individual income taxes delivered at least $26.3 billion to Albany during the 2025–2026 fiscal year, nearly 29% more than the prior year.

For employees, the implications are particularly lucrative. Provided markets remain relatively stable, DiNapoli believes the industry's enormous earnings could translate into unprecedented year-end compensation and bonus distributions in early 2027.

But the report also highlights a potential vulnerability beneath the financial windfall. Rising prices, international instability and technological changes associated with AI could eventually undermine the industry's performance.

And because New York now collects so much of its revenue from financial-sector activity, a sharp reversal on Wall Street would have consequences extending well beyond bankers and traders. A significant decline in profitability could quickly translate into weaker tax collections, pressure on public budgets and broader economic difficulties throughout the region.

title: Franklin Templeton Warns: No One Is Ready For A Eurozone Debt Crisis 2.0
desc:
Franklin Templeton Warns: No One Is Ready For A Eurozone Debt Crisis 2.0

New curfews in major French cities have helped contain the weeks of social unrest marked by far-left radicals and migrants burning buildings, looting mom-and-pop and luxury stores, and clashing with police. President Emmanuel Macron's failing government still faces another emerging issue: an alarming debt burden and a welfare state on the brink of collapse, addicted to decades of large deficits.

Franklin Templeton's chief investment officer for fixed income, Sonal Desai, warned that deteriorating finances could ignite another euro-area debt crisis, potentially harder to contain than the turmoil surrounding Greece.

"France has more than 10 times the debt that Greece had," Desai said in a webinar earlier today. "A simple bailout is not on the cards."

"I don't think anyone is really ready for a euro-zone debt crisis version 2.0," Desai added. "This one could be significantly worse if it were to come to pass."

She said investors shouldn't underestimate the potential for "significant volatility" in EU government bond markets. She added that Franklin Templeton's bond portfolios are positioned toward shorter-duration assets in Italy and France but have longer-duration investments in Spanish and German debt.

Earlier today, French borrowing costs climbed as investors demanded a larger premium to hold the nation's debt. This suggests mounting concerns over its debt load.

The extra yield investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over German debt widened to 154 basis points, the highest since early October.

"Bond markets now have much more choice over who they allocate to," said Karen Ward, chief market strategist for EMEA at JPMorgan Asset Management. "What we're seeing in France is just the bond market having this all-powerful role of having other options."

Bloomberg pointed out the possibility of European Central Bank intervention. ECB Governing Council member Olli Rehn said that all euro-area countries, including France, must bring deficits under control to ensure debt sustainability.

Jens Nordvig, president and co-founder of Vanda, warned earlier on Bloomberg TV that French spreads could widen even more.

"That cohesion, that political cooperation that is necessary for the bailout infrastructure to really work, is under pressure," Nordvig said.

In what could signal what's to come, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said today that he doesn't anticipate a spillover from the French bond market.

"I don't anticipate a spillover from what's happening in France," Bessent said on conservative platform 2Way. "The French have a tough hand, but President Macron's economic team, whom I know very well, are really first-rate."

title: BBC Game Rewards Kids For Supporting Open Borders
desc:
BBC Game Rewards Kids For Supporting Open Borders

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity.news,

The BBC’s education platform, used by nearly 1.7 million schoolchildren every week, is gamifying open borders. In a Roblox-hosted game called Increasing Immigration aimed at pupils aged 11 to 14, choosing to deport migrants living in the UK without proper visas loses points on the economy and public health.

Players are warned: “This can be potentially dangerous for them [the immigrants]. Don’t expect this to be unchallenged!”

Grant them an amnesty instead and the message is clear. “This will make them very happy.” Economy and public health scores rise.

BBC Bitesize is ‘indoctrinating’ and ‘brainwashing’ children. On @GBNEWS Here is what I’ve found ? https://t.co/qVezrC4kcf

— Alex Armstrong (@Alexarmstrong) October 18, 2026

A separate scenario tells geography pupils that allowing people to pass through the border easily “could really help grow our economy.” Selecting open borders yields three economy points and two public health points. Rejecting it as “too radical” scores nothing.

Instructions open with the claim: “We don’t have enough people of working age to keep our society running smoothly. We should try to attract migrant workers and incorporate them into our economy.”

Materials elsewhere state that concerns migrants will take jobs from locals “likely arises from prejudice.” The site lists twice as many benefits of migration as disadvantages.

Housing set aside for migrants scores positively. Almost every option aligned with border control produces negative results.

BBC Bitesize is promoted by almost every UK state school and reaches half of children aged four to 16.

Nick Timothy MP called it what it is.

This is indoctrination. Why are the BBC promoting open borders in a game for children? Deport illegal migrants and you lose points, but let them stay and a lawyer says it will make them “very happy.” I don’t care about making illegal migrants happy. They should be deported. And the BBC must take this game down.

— Nick Timothy MP (@NJ_Timothy) October 18, 2026

Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott demanded the game be removed. “The BBC has crossed a line. They have a duty to remain impartial, and yet they are using learning tools as a vehicle to push a Left-wing political agenda onto young children. Advocating open borders encourages illegal small boat crossings. These are the type of toxic resources dressed up as education which should be nowhere near the classroom.”

Former Education Secretary Gavin Williamson was more direct: “The mask has slipped and the BBC has yet again betrayed its rampant Left-wing political agenda. The state broadcaster brainwashing children using a homework game is like something from a North Korean re-education camp.”

Alex Burghart, Shadow Cabinet Office Secretary, said the BBC was set up “to inform, educate and entertain – not misinform, re-educate and brainwash.”

Former BBC Television controller Danny Cohen called for an investigation: “The BBC needs to explain why its educational website is pushing extreme Left-wing ideologies to schoolchildren… There is such a lack of balance… it cannot be seriously defended as coincidental.”

He added that “parents ought to be deeply concerned that the BBC is encouraging children to conform to extreme ideas such as open borders. It is yet another unacceptable failure of the BBC’s requirement to ensure impartiality.”

A BBC spokesman said the service works with educational consultants to align with curricula, does not accept the characterisation, regularly reviews content, and will review these examples. Director-general Matt Brittin has spoken of tools to monitor bias while the corporation faces charter renewal and declining licence-fee take-up.

This is not an isolated homework tool. It sits inside a broader pattern of materials that treat border control and concern about rapid demographic change as the problem to be solved rather than a legitimate policy choice.

Schools have distributed worksheets that place critics of mass migration alongside Nazis.

Government-funded games under the Prevent programme have warned children that researching immigration statistics, questioning job impacts, or protesting changes in Britain can place them on a pathway toward extremism referrals.

Classroom books have told primary pupils there is plenty of room for small-boat arrivals.

The Green Party has proposed teaching materials that frame opposition to high migration levels in the same category as extremism.

BBC children’s output has given activist groups direct access to shape storylines, and its flagship soap has carried pro-migrant messaging produced with campaign input.

The same institution that docks points for deportation in a children’s game has previously handed external campaigners the ability to influence what young viewers see.

Welsh geography materials on Bitesize have asked whether technology can help deliver “a truly borderless world.”

Net Zero content encourages pupils to petition local government and change personal behaviour. Progressive icons and movements are presented positively while dissenting views on migration are labelled prejudice.

Parents and taxpayers are not required to accept that a licence-fee-funded service used for homework is the appropriate vehicle for teaching that controlling the border is the radical option. The pattern across schools, government programmes, and BBC output is consistent: materials that normalise high migration and treat opposition as prejudice or extremism. The game simply makes the scoring visible.

The BBC says it will review the examples. Review is not the same as removal. Until the content is taken down or rewritten to present border control and amnesty as competing policy choices with equal weight and no predetermined point scores, the charge of one-sided instruction stands.

title: For restaurants Covid-19 was a crisis – pandemic loans are proving a disaster
desc:
Low-interest loans kept many eateries afloat. But the industry never recovered enough for them to repay the debt

For almost 20 years, Jai Mazumdar has served vegetarian curries, samosas, gulab jamun and other Indian delicacies at Spice N Curry, a cafe and grocery nestled inside a modest strip mall near Florida International University (FIU) in Miami. When the Covid-19 pandemic devastated his business, as it did with so many restaurants, Mazumdar took out a $370,000 economic injury disaster loan (EIDL) from the federal government in early 2021.

At the time, it provided a desperately needed lifeline. He was confident that once business returned to normal he could begin repaying the 30-year loan, which came with a low 3.75% interest rate and a 30-month deferment period. But when his business didn’t recover, the disaster loan turned out to be a disaster of its own.

title: ‘Countries are defying gravity’: how much longer can global economy resist chaos?
desc:
Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to last

Inside the vast, glass-walled Queen Sirikit conference centre in Bangkok, the air-conditioned atmosphere was calm as policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered this week for the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting – and contemplated the surprising strength of the global economy.

A small army of smiling, uniformed Thai staff were on hand to explain the baffling geography of the heavily guarded building, where lunch options were as cosmopolitan as the delegates – including, improbably, a Burger King.
